opus-5.5.text:
I think it changes the problem quite fundamentally. In the older paradigm, inference was mostly about serving: a request comes in, you generate a few hundred or a few thousand tokens, you return the answer. The main goals were throughput, latency, and cost per token. Training and inference were almost two separate worlds.

Once you do post-training with agents, especially reinforcement learning on long-horizon tasks, inference becomes part of the training loop itself. Most of the compute in RL is actually spent on rollouts: the model has to act, call tools, read results, think again, and sometimes run for dozens or hundreds of turns before you get a reward. So the inference system is no longer just a product-serving layer. It's the engine that produces your training data, and its efficiency directly decides how fast your model can improve.

That brings in a few new requirements.

First, **very long and very uneven sequences**. Agent trajectories can be extremely long, and their lengths vary a lot. Some finish in a few steps, some run for a very long time. If you batch them naively, the long tail dominates and your GPUs sit idle waiting. So you need asynchronous rollout, better scheduling, partial rollouts, ways to keep hardware busy despite the long tail.

Second, **interaction with environments**. The model isn't just generating text; it's waiting on a sandbox, a code executor, a browser, a search API. The inference architecture has to handle these pauses gracefully: keep KV cache around, or offload and restore it efficiently, so you're not recomputing the whole context every time a tool returns. Prefix caching and KV cache management become first-class concerns rather than optimizations.

Third, **consistency between training and inference**. In RL, if the inference engine computes probabilities slightly differently from the training framework, because of different kernels, precision, or parallelism, you get an off-policy mismatch that can quietly destabilize training. So now people care a lot about numerical alignment between the two stacks, which nobody worried much about when inference was only for serving.

Fourth, **weight synchronization**. The policy updates continuously, so you need to push new weights to a large fleet of inference workers quickly, sometimes while rollouts are still in flight. That's a systems problem in its own right.

And finally, I think it changes **model architecture choices**. If you know your model will spend its life in long, multi-turn agent loops, you start designing for that from the beginning: attention mechanisms that are cheaper over long context, efficient KV representations, MoE configurations that work well at the batch sizes you actually see in rollouts. So the boundary between model design, training system, and inference system becomes much blurrier. You really have to co-design them.

So my short answer is: inference used to be the last step of the pipeline. With agentic post-training, it's in the middle of the pipeline, and it's often the bottleneck. Teams that treat it that way, as a core part of research rather than an engineering afterthought, will iterate much faster.

r001.rationale: The response describes new requirements and says model, training, and inference should be co-designed, but it does not say those requirements are difficult to plan fully in advance.

r002.rationale: It calls inference the engine producing training data and a frequent bottleneck, but does not identify the model’s inference engine as the central architectural concern for chat-based reasoning.

r003.rationale: It explains that models designed for long, multi-turn agent loops need agent-aware choices and concludes that model and system design must be co-designed.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it changes the problem almost completely, and most of the inference stacks people built two years ago weren't designed for it.

When inference was just serving a chat model, the job was simple to state: take a prompt, produce tokens as fast and cheaply as possible, and keep latency predictable. You optimized throughput, you optimized KV cache, you batched aggressively. The requests were independent and short-lived, and once a response was done it was done.

Once you couple post-training with agents, you have at least three things that break that picture.

The first is that the rollout becomes the training signal. In reinforcement learning on agentic tasks, the model is interacting with an environment, calling tools, reading results, deciding again, maybe for dozens or hundreds of steps. The trajectory that comes out of inference is not a product for a user, it's data for the next gradient step. So inference and training can no longer be two separate systems that hand off a dataset once a week. They have to be in the same loop. The inference side has to be able to generate at enormous scale, with sampling diversity, with the ability to branch, to restart from an intermediate state, to attach rewards, and to feed that back quickly enough that the policy you're sampling from isn't already stale.

The second is that the unit of work is no longer a request, it's a trajectory with state. Agents have long contexts that grow, tool calls that may block for seconds or minutes, and lots of shared prefixes between parallel attempts at the same problem. If your scheduler thinks in terms of isolated requests, you waste an enormous amount of compute recomputing shared prefixes and holding memory for sessions that are waiting on an external tool. So the architecture needs to treat the KV cache almost like a first-class object, something that can be persisted, forked, resumed, and reused across rollouts. Prefix sharing, session suspension, and asynchronous tool execution stop being optimizations and become the core design.

The third is that the environment itself becomes part of the infrastructure. For a chat model, the "environment" is a human typing. For an agent, it's a sandbox, a code executor, a browser, a database, sometimes a simulated world. Those environments need to be spun up and torn down at the scale of the rollouts, they need to be isolated so one bad trajectory can't contaminate another, and they need to be deterministic enough that a reward actually means something. So suddenly the inference system is also orchestrating thousands of containers. That's a very different engineering culture from writing fast attention kernels.

And underneath all of it is a tension between training and inference that gets sharper. For stable RL you want the sampling policy and the training policy to be as close as possible, numerically. But inference engines use all sorts of tricks, different precision, different kernels, speculative decoding, that make the distribution subtly different from what the trainer thinks it's optimizing. In the chat world nobody cared. In the RL world, that mismatch shows up directly as instability or as the model learning to exploit artifacts. So you end up needing much tighter co-design between the two systems, sometimes down to sharing kernels or verifying logprob consistency.

So if I compress it: inference used to be a serving problem, and it's becoming a data-generation and systems-orchestration problem. The metrics shift from tokens per second toward useful trajectories per hour, and from latency toward how fast the whole loop closes. The teams that do well on this are the ones who stop treating post-training and inference as separate departments and build them as one system with one owner.

r001.rationale: It says agent post-training changes the problem and old inference stacks were not designed for it, but does not say the requirements are difficult to plan fully in advance.

r002.rationale: It describes conventional chat inference as a serving and optimization problem, but does not identify the model’s inference engine as the central architectural concern for chat-based reasoning.

r003.rationale: It treats the model’s interaction with tools and environments as part of inference, and says the system must orchestrate those environments alongside rollouts.

astra-6.text:
I think it changes the unit we’re optimizing for. With a chatbot, we often focus on one response: how quickly the model starts generating and how efficiently it produces tokens. With an agent, the unit is a whole task. The model takes an action, gets feedback from a tool or environment, and decides what to do next. Inference has to support that entire loop.

When you couple this with post-training, the loop becomes part of learning as well. You need to generate trajectories, evaluate outcomes, and use that feedback to improve the policy. So the inference architecture needs efficient state management, tool execution, and scheduling across workloads where some requests are generating while others are waiting on the environment.

The interesting part is that training and infrastructure choices become interdependent. If training teaches the model to explore several alternatives, inference needs to support branching efficiently. If tool feedback is slow, generating tokens faster may barely improve task completion time.

So I would look beyond tokens per second. What matters is how reliably the system completes a task, at what cost, and within what latency. That gives you a different target for designing the architecture.

r001.rationale: The response says training and infrastructure choices are interdependent, but does not state that iterative agent development makes inference requirements difficult to plan fully in advance.

r002.rationale: It contrasts chatbot token generation with agent task loops, but does not identify the model’s inference engine as the central architectural concern for chat-based reasoning.

r003.rationale: It describes agent inference as a loop involving model actions, tool or environment feedback, and next decisions, and identifies supporting that loop as an architectural requirement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it changes inference from generating a single answer into managing a whole process. An agent takes an action, observes what happened, and decides what to do next. So the inference architecture has to support that loop: tool calls, persistent state, and trajectories that may take very different amounts of time to complete.

When you couple that with post-training, those trajectories also become training data. You need to capture more than the final answer—you need the actions, observations, and signals about whether the task succeeded. Otherwise, it’s difficult to understand which decisions actually improved the outcome.

That creates an interesting tradeoff. During training, you want to generate useful experience efficiently. During deployment, you care about latency, cost, and reliability. I think the architecture needs to support both, with a consistent interface between the model and its environment, so the behavior you train is the behavior you can actually serve.

r001.rationale: The response describes the needs of agent inference, but does not say those requirements are difficult to plan fully in advance.

r002.rationale: It does not identify the model’s inference engine as the central concern for chat-based reasoning.

r003.rationale: It calls for a consistent interface between the model and its environment so trained behavior matches what can be served, communicating the model-agent coupling concern.
